1271340,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.7.2,1942-05-27,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,HONG KONG COMMISSION-GEORGE DREW,,,There has been no arrangement between the government and Mr. George Drew, K.C., for attending the Hong Kong inquiry commission.

Pursuant to section 11 of the Inquiries Act, chapter 99 Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, a commissioner appointed under the act has full authority to engage counsel to aid and assist in the inquiry. This power is specifically mentioned in P.C. 1160, February 12, 1942, appointing the Right Hon. Sir Lyman Poore Duff, P.C., C.M.G., a commissioner under the Inquiries Act.

,Liberal,,Mr. WINKLER:,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=81c6273a-3e4d-4184-a386-e74f813aaac8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1271343,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.8.2,1942-05-27,0bd1c7bb-8591-4517-b5ff-c82c3ab12753,ca.m.8077,,Minister of National War Services,NATIONAL WAR SERVICES-COMMITTEE ON COOPERATION IN CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP,,,1. There is no cultural relations committee in the Department, so named, but there is a committee on cooperation in Canadian citizenship. The. chairman of this committee is Professor G. W. Simpson, senior adviser to the Director of Public Information. Professor Simpson has been connected with the University of Saskatchewan for nineteen years and is, at present, head of the Department of History. Mr. Tracy Philipps, adviser to the Director of Public Information, is European adviser of the committee. He is an expert on recent political conditions in southern and eastern Europe. The members of the committee are as follows:
Professor H. F. Angus, of the University of British Columbia, now attached to the Department of External Affairs, appointed December 13, 1941.
Honourable C. H. Blakeny, Minister of Education in New Brunswick, appointed December 10, 1941.
Major J. S. A. Bois, Professor of Philosophy, University of Montreal, now personnel consultant in the Canadian army, appointed December 31, 1941.
Professor Jean Bruchesi, author and educationalist, appointed April 14, 1942.
Mr. D. Cameron, Director of Extension Work, University of Alberta, appointed December 27, 1941.
Dr. S. D. Clark, Lecturer in Sociology, University of Toronto, appointed January 15, 1942.
Mr. Robert England, Department of Pensions and National Health, executive secretary to the rehabilitation committee, appointed December 11, 1941.
Mr. J. Murray Gibbon, author of ""Canadian Mosaic"", appointed December 9, 1941.
Professor Watson Kirkconnell, Professor of Literature, McMaster University, appointed December 10, 1941.
Mr. Tracy Philipps, D.C.L., F.R.I.A., foreign diplomatic correspondent, appointed November 27, 1941; salary, $4,392 per annum.
Mrs. R. F. McWilliams, fromer Winnipeg city councillor and social worker, appointed December 12, 1941.
Professor G. W. Simpson, head of the History Department, University of Saskatchewan, appointed November 1, 1941; salary, $4,500 per annum.
Mrs. O. D. Skelton, author and educationalist, appointed February 4, 1942.
All members, except where otherwise stated, serve without salary, but all receive out-ofpocket travelling expenses incurred while on official business of the committee.

1271345,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.9.1,1942-05-27,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICE PERSONNEL LISTED IN DEFENCE TELEPHONE DIRECTORY,,,I should like to submit an answer to a question which, though -it did not appear on the order paper, was asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) on May 11, during the course of the debate on the appropriation bill, and appears at page 2292 of Hansard. It has reference to the number of bilingual employees whose names are listed in the telephone directory.

So far as the naval service is concerned, there are 326 names listed in the directory in question. Of these, 280 have resided in Canada during the past 5 years, of whom 60 are bilingual and 220 are not bilingual. Eleven persons listed have not resided in Canada for the past 5 years, and of this number one is bilingual and 10 are not bilingual. Thirty-five naval officers whose names appear in the directory have been drafted away from naval service headquarters since the directory list was prepared and details are not available.

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,HONG KONG COMMISSION,INQUIRY AS TO PRESENTATION OF REPORT,,There is only one person I know of in the world who can answer that question, and that is the chief justice who is the commissioner. The chief justice, I am sure, has been giving his closest attention to the proceedings of the commission and, as has been explained two or three times in the house, he has been obliged to wait until one of the counsel who appeared before him had an opportunity to file a brief which the chief justice was prepared to consider before making a final report. 1271415,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.25.1.1.1,1942-05-27,,,,stagedirection,,,,On the orders of the day:

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Yesterday I promised to give an answer to a question put to me by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) on May 21 concerning a speech reported to have been delivered in Montreal by Mr. Rene Chaloult.

The legal advisers of the Department of Justice have informed me that in their opinion the speech made in Montreal by Mr. Rene Chaloult on the evening of May 19, as reported in the newspapers, clearly disclosed a seditious intention, and constitutes an offence against the defence of Canada regulations; and I agree with that conclusion. They have also called my attention to the fact that Mr. Chaloult, speaking in the legislative assembly of the province of Quebec on May 22 on a question of privilege, stated that the newspaper reports of this speech were not strictly accurate, and conveyed an impression which was not warranted by the language he had used.

In view of this dispute as to the facts, it has been decided to institute proceedings against Mr. Chaloult under the defence of Canada regulations, in the district in which the offence is alleged to have been committed.

So that there may be no misunderstanding about the policy of the department under the defence of Canada regulations, I wish to add that this decision does not mean that there has been any departure from the policy of ordering detention as provided for by the defence of Canada regulations when that is found to be necessary. Seditious conduct or utterances cannot be tolerated. During peace-time the procedure for repression is prosecution before the courts under the criminal code; during wartime there may be prosecution before the courts or detention.
Everyone is agreed that in such a case as this, prosecution before the courts is the preferable method, when it can be looked upon as sufficiently effective. But the repression must

be effective, and when it appears that prosecution before the courts does not produce the desired result, or does not produce it with sufficient dispatch, the interests of the state require that detention be resorted to; and in these last mentioned circumstances detention will continue to be resorted to.",,,,

1271422,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.2,1942-05-27,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,"I want to refer briefly
to an answer that the minister gave yesterday to a question asked by the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence). As reported at page 2802 of Hansard, the minister said:
It is only within the last twelve or fifteen years that crude oil has been developed in Alberta.
Further on:

There was one other point raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon City. There was a question whether any dominion leases were outstanding on the tar sands in northern Alberta. I speak subject to correction, but my definite impression is that no dominion leases are outstanding on those tar sands. Any leases that have been issued were issued subsequent to the transfer of the resources to Alberta.

I believe the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were created in 1905. Between 1905 and 1930 the natural resources were administered by the dominion government, that is until some twelve years ago. I wonder whether the minister's statement was correct. I have in my hand what I presume are minutes of the company that operated the Murphy claim on the Athabaska river, sent to me some few months ago when I first began to get ready to make a speech on the Alberta tar sands. The book is entitled, ""Particulars of Tar Sand Lease No. 15 known as the 'Murphy Claim', Alberta, Canada."" This company- must have been operating long before 1930, and to have operated it must have had a lease from the dominion government. On page 47 of this book I notice a picture illustrating the laying of a roadway in the city of Edmonton in 1915. The picture is entitled, ""Beginning to lay asphaltic concrete from 'Murphy claim' on Kinnaird street, Edmonton, Alberta"". That claim I believe is some thirty to forty miles down the Athabaska river from Fort McMurray.

Farther down the river there is another claim that has been operated for years, the Fitzsimmons claim. I am sure the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) will be thoroughly familiar with that. From what I saw there I imagine that this later claim has been operating for more than ten or twelve years. They have shipped a large
Alberta Natural Resources
quantity of material from that claim. When I was there last summer they were shipping several hundred barrels.

To come back to the claim of which I have full particulars before me, the Murphy claim, that goes to show that there must have been leases prior to 1915, for the company had been in production and had shipped material to Edmonton and, I believe, other cities in the western provinces.
I read on page 51 of these minutes the following:

Certified copy of regulations for the disposal of the tar sands, the property of the crown, in that portion of the province of Alberta lying north of township 80, and between the fourth and fifth initial meridians.
Approved by order in council, dated the 14th of February, 1910.
Therefore from 1910 on the dominion government must have issued leases for the development of the tar sands, either to obtain oil or bitumen or asphalt, all of which come from the tar sands.
A note follows, which reads:
These regulations will come into effect on Saturday, the 19th day of March, 1910. . . .
Then on page 52 I read:

The tar sand deposits which are the property of the crown in that portion of the province of Alberta lying north of township 80, and between the fourth and fifth initial meridians, may be leased to applicants for a term of twenty-one years at an annual rental of 50 cents an acre, payable yearly in advance. The term of the lease shall be twenty-one years, renewable for a further twenty-one years.

I presume that would be under the conditions enumerated herein. This would mean that anyone obtaining a lease at that time could have had that lease for forty-two years, and I am just wondering if any of these leases are still in effect. If they are, perhaps that would have some bearing on the bill now before the committee, or perhaps not; I do not know, but I thought I should inform the committee that the leases were renewable, since I believe this lease is the same as all others which were issued at that time. Then I quote from page 55:
In case the tract applied for is located on the margin of a river or lake-*
This particular lease covered an area on the Athabaska river.

-it shall not include more than one mile in direct distance along such water frontage, and shall be marked on the ground by two legal posts firmly fixed in the ground, one at each end of such front boundary.

This particular lease extended back from the river for a distance of three miles, and included within its boundaries some 1,920 acres, which I believe is the maximum that could be granted. That is a fairly large grant,

in any event, since we have been told by engineers that an acre of 100 per cent tar sand should contain approximately 70,000 barrels, which would give a large, volume of oil, bitumen or asphalt. So that was a fairly substantial lease. Whether or not it is still in existence I do not know, but on page 58 I notice this clause, providing that leases may be transferred:
The leases shall not assign, transfer, or sublet the rights described in his lease, or any part thereof, without the consent in writing of the minister being first had and obtained.

So a lease could be transferred from one person to another, and I understand that was done with this particular lease. I believe it is now in the possession of an operator who is about to develop it, because when I went north on the river last summer a gentleman, a geologist and engineer, got off the boat. I understood he was getting off in the vicinity of the Murphy claim, from which I took it that his principals must have secured the renewal of some previous lease covering the point at which this gentleman left the boat.

I do not know what regulations were introduced by the provinces after they secured the return of their natural resources in 1930, but on page 59 of this volume I find this paragraph with regard to royalties:
No royalty shall be charged upon the products of any tar sand location granted under these regulations, or on the sales of the products of such location up to the 1st day of January, 1930-

That would be prior to the provinces taking possession of their natural resources. I do not know the exact date when the act to return the natural resources was passed, but it was some time in 1930, so they must have come into possession of the resources some time after January 1.

-but provision shall be made in the lease issued for such location that after the above date, the products of the location shall be subject to whatever regulations in respect of the payment of royalty may then or thereafter be made.

Whether the regulations put into effect by the dominion government were retained by the provinces after 1930, I do not know; but it may be that those holding these leases on January 1, 1930, were able to have them renewed on the same terms that existed before January 1, 1930. Then in the latter part of his reply to the hon. member for Saskatoon City last evening, the minister said:
Any leases that have been issued were issued subsequent to the transfer of the resources to Alberta.
If what I have just read is correct, would the minister's statement also be correct? I
Alberta Natural Resources

know he qualified what he said by saying that it was according to his best information, or something like that; but what I have read indicates that leases were granted while the dominion government retained possession of the natural resources, that those leases could be transferred, and that they could be extended for a total period of forty-two years, which would bring them up to 1952. Whether or not the bill now before the committee should be amended to protect leases made prior to the return of the natural resources is something I cannot say. But, Mr. Chairman, having this information in my possession, I thought I should place it upon Hansard.

,National Government,,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL

As far as I am aware that was the only lease outstanding. It was not given, however, for the purpose of developing oil. Again I am speaking subject to Correction, because I have not had an opportunity to get all the facts in connection with the matter, but at that time it was thought that these tar sands provided a natural road surfacing material; that is, if you could take the tar sands, with the amount of bitumen they contained, and transport them and surface a road with them, you would have a good surfacing material. That was done in order to test its durability, and it appears there is no question now as to the quality of this material for hard surfacing roads. At that time, however, the purpose was to use the material for hard surfacing, and not for the extraction of oil.

I believe it was recognized from the first that these tar sands had potential oil value. The problem was to find a formula for treating the sands so as to extract the oil. I recall that the university of Alberta carried on laboratory experiments for some time in an effort to determine a method of extracting the oil from the sand. If my information is correct, it had in its early stages rather doubtful success; but as time went on the resources of science applied itself to the problem, with the result that within comparatively recent years a process, although perhaps not a perfect one, has been discovered for extracting the oil from the sands. As a matter of fact, a company was operating for this purpose on a modest scale near Waterways, and had some degree of success in extracting oil from these sands.

It is obvious to members of the committee familiar with the geography of the district that the handicap in developing this as a eom-merical proposition arises from the fact that it is so remote from the centres of population.

1271433,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.13,1942-05-27,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,May I add one further word to what the minister has said? I made a very careful survey covering several days, and my observation was that the difficulty was not that of taking the oil out of the sand. That, in fact, was a very simple matter. The difficuty to overcome-and it has been overcome-was one of getting the sand out of the mine. The sands were shaved off, and the sand itself, a sample of which I have in my hand, acted like a sand blast. In the business in which I was engaged we used sand blasts, and I know that sand blasts will cut right through steel. Therefore, as the shavers or scrapers went round and round on a wheel belt the sand would wear them out. That was the biggest part of the difficulty.

May I add in passing, that the department is greatly blessed in having a man like Doctor S. C. Ells in its employ. I believe it was Doctor Ells who discovered the system of taking the oil out of the sand. It is a simple process which involves the use of hot water, and when this process is used the oil can be taken out in two minutes. I have often said to myself that the Minister of Mines and Resources has a wonderful opportunity to develop the resources of this 'country when he has in his department a capable oil expert like Doctor Ells. I know if I were minister I would be inclined to send Doctor Ells up to the Athabaska district, with instructions to produce oil. I am sure he would produce it in quantities sufficient to warrant the building of a pipeline to Edmonton.

,National Government,,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1271434,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.14,1942-05-27,b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442,ca.m.5903,Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury):,Leader of the Official Opposition,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,The minister has never brought down the correspondence for which I asked in March, and which I understood was to have been brought down. I would assume that there has been a considerable amount of correspondence between him or his department, the government of Alberta and the leaseholders. I should not be surprised if in that correspondence between the minister and the leaseholders, or those representing the leaseholders, the question of breach of trust was not raised. Under those circumstances I suggest we ought to have the correspondence. Furthermore it would not be surprising if in that correspondence the minister himself was gravely concerned about the question of breach of trust, and raised that question in correspondence with the government of Alberta. Following along that line of thought, I would not be surprised if that
was one of the main reasons why the minister did not proceed with'this legislation last year. I would ask him to state quite frankly what happened on that point.

This morning I read over somewhat hastily the observations made last night by the minister, but I could not find any place where he dealt adequately with the question I have raised. Undoubtedly in law, by reason of the circumstances which have arisen, in a degree the dominion has been occupying a fiduciary position. That fiduciary position will be lifted if this bill is passed and confirmation is given to the agreement between the dominion and the province. That agreement, as a schedule to the bill, is part and parcel of the legislation. When the bill is passed, the last refuge of those who have complained against the legislation will be gone; all their protection will have vanished, and they will be at the mercy of the provincial administration. At that time, of course, the provincial administration will be free to do whatever it likes.

I suggest that the minister ought to tell us whether this theory-possibly it is more than a theory-this cogent argument against what he is now doing was not raised directly by the parties and interests who, I shall not say will be the victims, but will be placed under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities with respect to leases for petroleum rights originally issued by the dominion over this area. I would ask if that question did not seriously affect the minister's judgment. Is that not one reason why he refused to proceed last year, and one reason which actuated him, if I understand his statement correctly, when he sought to get the consent of these parties. In that connection I think the minister ought to tell us how many leases were issued by his department prior to the transfer and were outstanding in 1941. I mean those that were in good working order, those in connection with which the leaseholders had paid the annual fee or whatever was required by the department even though they might not be operating. I understood there were some 810 leases. That is the number outstanding at the time of the transfer of the resources, but I should like to know how many are still outstanding and might be said to be in good standing legally. Then I should like to compare that number with the number of lease owners who are alleged-I am going to use that word

or who it is said have agreed to this legislation. I think it will be found that a large number have never agreed. If they have not agreed they may be prejudicially affected by this legislation. The position occupied by the federal authority still stands with respect to them.
Alberta Natural Resources

This matter has attracted a good deal of attention in the west, and I have had some representations made to me, I suppose largely because of the newspaper reports of the discussion that took place yesterday. This morning I was in receipt of a telegram from a gentleman whom I do not know but who signs himself Robert Wilkinson, and who, I understand, is president of the National Petroleum Corporation Limited of Calgary. As far as I know, this man has not been consulted, and according to his observations he certainly has not given his consent. His telegram reads:

Regarding debate Alberta oil royalty situation operators here strongly support your opposition to passage of this measure particularly now when every encouragement should be given producers and those providing finances for new development. Ten large rotary drilling rigs now idle, all owned by independent operators. Please refer letter editorial page Toronto Star dated 15th July, 1941.
Then he makes reference to Hansard but I could not find the page to which he refers. And the telegram concludes:
Suggest that passage of bill in present form *Bull be near approach to sabotage and must be effectively prevented.
That is how this man characterizes this legislation.

If I interpreted the remarks of the minister correctly, they were to the effect that this legislation would bring about stability and from that there would follow action with regard to the production of oil. This man's statement is entirely contrary to that. He wrote a letter to the Toronto Star on July 15, 1941, and I have a copy of that before me. It was entitled, ""Canada's Western Oil"", and in it he indicates the reasons why there is no development of these oil fields. He states that the reason for this is the fact that the basic price has been put down so low having regard to the cost of operating that the independent operators cannot go on. He refers to the increased cost of drilling and so forth. He stated that there was $2,000,000 worth of equipment now idle. This position is not due to the position of the leases. This stagnation is due to the low prices which have been set by the oil controller or by some authority as the basic price for crude in the Turner valley field.

I do so first from the legal point of view and, second, as a matter of public policy. It is strange the enthusiasm of the present minister for this proposed variation. your nose, as the hon. member for Temiscouata said one day, without its being said it is for the war. You can scarcely blow your nose now anyway because we have dollar-a-year men limiting the length of your handkerchief.

The principle of law in this variation transfer has been before the privy council in what was known as the Alberta great waterways case, which was on all fours with the proposed agreement. The law is quite clear. The crown in the name of the dominion or the crown in the name of the province cannot vary agreements or contracts or bonds or any such matters. They may do it in British Honduras; this variation agreement is almost on a parallel with the Alberta privy council case to which I referred, but the decision of the privy council in the great waterways case was the ground on which the bill of sale was based when the province of Ontario purchased the $32,000,000 property of the power companies in the Niagara district. All the papers in this new agreement matter should be tabled. Who is asking for this thing? There are 860 leases affected by this agreement. Did the holders of any of them object? If one objected, that one on behalf of himself and the other leaseholders could enter action against the attorneys general of the province and the dominion to set aside the proposed transfer in view of the decision of the privy council.

I oppose this measure on other grounds. We have a supreme court in Canada. Under the Supreme Court Act it is the duty and function of the government, where vested rights are involved as in this particular transfer agreement; it is not only the duty but one of the functions of the Attorney General of Canada, that is the present Minister of Justice who is measuring up as a great lawyer and a gentleman who, I believe, will be a great Minister of Justice, to refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada.

The functions and duties of the government in transfer agreement cases of this kind are set out in the decisions of the privy council to which I referred. Under the Supreme Court Act it is the function of the government of the day, where doubt has arisen, to refer the matter for the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada. There is doubt in this case; both governments knew they had no power to vary these contracts legally and so make an agreement as a matter of policy. If they did not know that they would not have framed this bill in this language. They knew the courts would set it aside, on the ground that the government had no right to vary a contract in the manner indicated. A reference should have been made to the Supreme Court of Canada, and in less than three months a

decision on the text of the reference would have been given. It was bad enough in peace time to squander the natural resources of this country, the products of the sea, the soil, the forest, the mine and so on. I hope the hon. gentleman will not leave

1271526,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.106,1942-05-27,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,If you would also leave the agreement alone it might be better for the resources of the country, or if you would leave the decision to the people. Where do the people who own this property come in? The dominion government is simply the trustee of the public domain of this country. Our natural resources have been squandered so much that future generations will wonder what kind of people were sitting in this parliament to allow that to go on. I remember 1927, when it was proposed to hand over the natural resources of the whole Ottawa valley to the Sifton interests. We were in opposition at that time; we started a debate and talked out the bill, so that it did not go through. If it had gone through, all the resources of this great Ottawa valley would have been handed over forever to private greed and gain.

This is the second war session we have done something in the way of giving away the natural resources of Alberta in the name of the war. Last session a bill was introduced by the Minister of Mines and Resources having to do with power development in Banff national park. Considerable discussion took place on that bill, and many questions of law and public policy were raised. At the time, in 1927, the Ottawa valley matter was under consideration I quoted some of the words of the late President Theodore Roosevelt and the late Sir Adam Beck on the need of a national policy for our resources. Perhaps I might recall what I quoted at that time. The late President Theodore Roosevelt said:

The people of our country are threatened by a monopoly more powerful than has ever been seen, as it affects very closely their domestic and industrial life. Our next generation will witness a shortage of those natural resources, petroleum and gas. The price of coal will be such that hydraulic power turned into electrical energy will, owing to its cost, become the prevailing factor for transport, for manufacturers, for lighting and heating our towns. Our hydraulic power alone, entirely and judicially employed, would be adequate for the present needs of transport, industries, municipalities and private individuals.
And Sir Adam Beck, in opposing the bill that would have given away those great natural resources which belong to the people of the whole dominion, said:
In my judgment, no government in Canada can stand against the opposition of the public
Alberta Natural Resources
opinion that will be expressed by the people of the provinces of Ontario and of Quebec once it is fully appreciated what sacrifice of their interests is involved. . . .

He was then referring to the giving away of the Carillon water power development on the Ottawa river, and the right to export power to the United States. Ever since I have been a member of this house I have been asking for a national policy with regard to oil, gas, coal and power. We have 42 million horse-power available in Canada of which less than one-sixth, or 7 million horse-power, has been developed, and of that a part is only seasonal. Here you are, giving away the heritage of the people without their authority or consent. I have also asked for a national policy in connection with coal. There was a debate in this house on that subject on my resolution for a national coal supply, all British, on March 18, 1923, and that discussion went on for ten years before anything was done about a coal supply from Alberta or the maritimes or Wales. We also had many debates, from 1923 on, on a policy of conserving the oil, coal and petroleum resources of Alberta and other parts of Canada. The government have had almost twenty years in which to formulate a policy. Why did they have to wait for a war to come along before doing anything about it? I agree with what was said in this chamber last evening by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) that notwithstanding the royalties, leases and all that sort of thing, the time now has come when instead of proposing amendments such as this the government should bring in a national policy with regard to coal, gas, oil and the power inherent in falling water. Here we are giving away these natural resources in the name of the war, and calling it conservation. What sort of conservation was it when we gave Japan large quantities of our resources of timber, pig iron, scrap iron, aluminum, nickel, platinum, copper and all the rest. Our natural resources were given to our enemies to make munitions for land, sea and air, who are making war against us on the seven seas.

I can tell you that one of these days, when this giving away of the heritage of the people is fully understood, there will be a rebellion in this country. Public opinion will be against such squandering of the public domain. This coming winter we are faced with a coal shortage, but what are we doing? We are sitting around here amending a transfer agreement that will bring about ten times as much litigation as we have had in the past, and Alberta since 1930 has had a lot of it.

As I have said, any or all of the 860 people holding these leases can issue a writ against the attorney general of the province and the dominion and have this whole agreement set aside. The people of Alberta should have voted on this deal, because I venture to say that in the years to come it will be regarded as just as iniquitous as the Ottawa valley and other gifts of resources. What was refused in the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal principle of dealing with resources in the days of peace is now put forward as a conservation measure in days' of war. I do not believe a single gallon of oil will result from this agreement, because there is no doubt it will be taken to the law courts and kept there for years.

We had this matter of conservation and public ownership under discussion from 1902 to 1930, in Ontario, which finally has been redeemed from this sort of power slavery of private greed. I think every other province should do the same thing; for if it had not been for the power development in Ontario our effort in the last war would have been greatly reduced. At one time during that war fifty per cent of the munitions produced in the war came from Ontario, thanks to the magnificent power reserves that were available here under public ownership at cost. I believe that if the dominion had had a national policy designed to preserve these natural resources of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mine; the coal resources, the oil and gas resources and the power resources, it would have been a blessing to the people of this country long before the war began, and it will come quickly, after the war. It belongs to the people.

1271534,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.114,1942-05-27,cd519f4c-2e6c-423f-a87d-fae814d3cad2,ca.m.1715,Mr. BENCE:,,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,I would point out in reference to the remarks of the minister that section 2 of the agreement dated December 14, 1929, contained the following statement with respect to the matter of leases:
. . . and further agrees-
That is, the provincial government.
-not to affect or alter any term of any such contract to purchase, lease or other arrangements by legislation or otherwise.
That is much broader than the minister has indicated to the committee. It covers not only the originally leased contracts, but any arrangement by legislation or otherwise.

Actually what happened in this instance was that in 1920 an order in council was passed for the specific purpose of giving stability to oil production in Alberta. That stability was given by virtue of the fact that the men who owned the leases knew definitely the amount they would have to pay, and knew it would not be exceeded by the amount set out in the order in council.

I suggest to the committee that if there were any instability, such instability was created by the action of Alberta, and that Alberta itself could easily stabilize the thing without the necessity of this legislation, by agreeing that section 2 did not give them the authority to change the royalties. If the province would agree to that, there would be no necessity for any litigation in the courts, no necessity for uncertainty in the minds of the leaseholders, and no necessity for members of this committee, who, I suggest, have only a meagre amount of information before them on which to base their judgments, to pass upon something which I contend, with the leader of the opposition, is definitely a breach of trust. After all. if there is any dispute in the courts as to whether Alberta was entitled to increase its royalties, surely it is not the duty of this parliament to settle the matter for the courts, and to place Alberta in the preferred position they have endeavoured to
obtain, by deliberately coming out and committing what I consider to be a breach of section 2 of the agreement.

I ask the minister to inform the committee as to whether or not that stability could be obtained just as easily if Alberta would take the action I have suggested. I would also ask him the question I propounded last night, namely, whether or not section 2 of the agreement dated December 14, 1929, was considered by the law officers of the Department of Justice, and whether the minister obtained an opinion from that department as to the reason for the incorporation of section 2 in the agreement at that time, and whether or not it was put in for the purpose of protecting the dominion government against possible action for damages. In the event of any uncertainty in the minds of the law officers of the Department of Justice as to the dominion's liability for damages, did the minister consider whether or not the dominion government should make itself liable for any damages which were actually incurred as a result of the passing of this legislation? I should like to have an answer. Was this matter referred to the Department of Justice and, if not, does the minister not think it should be referred before we pass upon it?

1271568,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.148,1942-05-27,a0f8dbd6-a310-4dd8-a89a-5dcdd30f0517,ca.m.6856,Mr. EDWARDS:,,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,There was one point the minister seemed to be quite sure about in his statement last night, and it is something over which I have been considerably exercised since. He referred to the undoubted power of the federal government to alter or change the terms and conditions of a lease by regulation after the lease had in fact been passed over to a private individual. This very matter has been the subject of judicial questioning only as recently as April of this year. The provisions of section 2 of the natural resources agreement came before the supreme court of Alberta in connection with the case of Anthony v. the attorney general of Alberta and the minister of lands and mines, reported at page 833 of volume 1 of 1942 ""Western Weekly Reports"". The question there was the right of the province to alter the terms and conditions or to refuse renewal of a timber lease which had been issued by the dominion government prior to the transfer of the natural resources, and which, therefore, came within the purview of the Alberta resources agreement, under this section 2 to which we are referring. I quote from the judgment. Referring to the Alberta government's order in council, it says:

The order in council of July 25, 1940, prohibiting renewal of timber licences for more than ten years after the date of sale affects or alters the plaintiffs' licences which are renewable while merchantable timber remains on the limits and is ultra vires as being contrary to section 2 of the natural resources agreement. I declare the said provision in the order in council to be invalid and ultra vires as against the plaintiffs.

That in turn is supported by no less an authority than the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Spooner Oils Limited vs. The Turner Valley gas conservation board and the attorney general of Alberta, which is cited in the Supreme Court Reports for the year 1933. With the permission of the Chair I would like to read what I consider is pertinent to the subject under discussion as found in the judgment of the Chief Justice of Canada. Here you had an oil and gas lease similar to the ones which are being discussed and which are contemplated by this very bill. I quote:

The lease declares, in express terms, that it is granted by the Minister of the Interior, pursuant to regulations made for the disposal of petroleum and natural gas rights, by orders in council dated respectively the 11th days of March, 1910 and 1911, ""a copy of which regulations is hereby appended"". The term is twenty-one years,-
Alberta Natural Resources
You will notice the language here is exactly that quoted by the minister:

-and the lease is ""renewable for a further term of twenty-one years provided the lessee furnishes evidence satisfactory to the Minister of the Interior to show that during the term of the lease he has complied fully with the conditions of such lease and with the provisions of the regulations under which it was granted"".
Among the ""provisos, conditions, restrictions and stipulations"" of the lease there is this:

(2) That the lessee shall and will well, truly and faithfully observe, perform and abide by all the obligations, conditions, provisos and restrictions in or under the said regulations imposed upon lessees or upon the said lessee.
The regulations ""appended"" to the lease contain the following:
That is the same form of lease that is still being issued.
21. The lease shall be in such form as may be determined by the Minister of the Interior, in accordance with the provisions of these regulations.

It appears that the lease is framed upon the view that the rights of the parties inter se are to be ascertained from the provisions of the lease, from the regulations, a copy of which is appended thereto, and such further orders and regulations and directions as may be made from time to time during the currency of the lease under article 9 of the lease or sections 23 and 24 of the regulations. The last mentioned sections are in these words:

23. No royalty shall be charged upon the sales of the petroleum acquired from the crown under the provisions of the regulations up to the 1st day of January, 1930, but provision shall be made in the leases issued for such rights that after the above date the petroleum products of the location shall be subject to whatever regulations in respect of the payment of royalty may then or thereafter be made.""
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury:) That is, by the dominion.

24. A royalty at such rate as may from time to time be specified by order in council may be levied and collected on the natural gas products of the leasehold.""
Note this, ""as may from time to time"".

But, it is argued that, notwithstanding the form of the lease itself, the concluding words of s. 1 of the regulations of 1910 and 1911 have the effect of incorporating, as conditions of the lease, all subsequent regulations made during the currency of the term. The sentence in *which these words occur is this:

The term of the lease shall be twenty-one years, renewable for a further term of twenty-one years, provided the lessee can furnish evidence satisfactory to the minister to show that during the term of the lease he has complied fully with the conditions of such lease and with the provisions of the regulations in force from time to time during the currency of the lease.""
The regulations in force from time to time during the currency of the lease"" should be read, it is argued, as embracing all subsequent
regulations whether incorporated in the terms of the lease, by force of some provision of the lease or of the existing regulations, or not.

It will be observed that the proviso, in express terms, affects only the right of renewal. On the supposition that the proviso relates to this right of renewal, and to that right alone, we arrive (on the construction advocated by the respondents) at the truly extraordinary result, that, even under the renewed lease, the lessee is not bound by s. 29; although his right of renewal is dependent upon compliance with that section prior to the completion of the original term. It is difficult, no doubt, to think it could have been intended that the lessee's right of renewal should be conditioned upon the performance, during the term antecedent to its renewal, of obligations which the lessee was not required to observe as contractual terms of the lease. But to us it seems clear that, if it had been intended to incorporate, as one of the terms of the lease, a stipulation that all future regulations touching the working of the property should become part of the lease as contractual stipulations, that intention would have been expressed, pot inferentially, but in plain language.

Alberta Natural Resources

1271615,ca.proc.d.1942-05-27.27.1.195,1942-05-27,2db22441-d3ea-4e76-8d18-f4753949bd74,ca.m.812,Mr. BLACKMORE:,,ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES,AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION,,Mr. Chairman, it

seems to me there are three or four matters involved in this question. The first one is this: Shall the province of Alberta have a right to her natural resources equivalent to the right each over her own natural resources
Alberta Natural Resources
possessed by New Brunswick, or by Ontario, or by Prince Edward Island? This bill is designed merely to confer upoD Alberta that right-and no more.

My second question is this: At the time the province of Alberta was formed had the dominion parliament the right to confer upon that province rights over her resources equivalent to the rights possessed and enjoyed by New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Ontario over theirs?

Third: If the dominion government did not possess that right, why not? If it did possess the right, then did it confer upon Alberta power over her resources equal to those possessed by New Brunswick? Then, if for any reason, through legal terminology or through any other deficiency whatsoever, the dominion government in making an endeavour to pass on to Alberta in 1930 rights equivalent to those possessed by New Brunswick, failed to do so -the dominion having the desire, but failing to carry out the intention-has the dominion government at the present time the right to remedy the defect, and to pass a measure which shall in effect transfer to Alberta sovereign rights over her resources, equivalent to those enjoyed by Prince Ediward Island?
If these questions are answered in the affirmative, then there is no doubt at all about the power of this parliament to pass this measure and to make it effective.

May I for a moment or two turn to the two cases cited by the hon. member for Calgary West. In listening to them for the first time one obviously had some difficulty in assessing them accurately. However, listening to those cases as they were being read, I gathered that the first one was not analogous at all, and did not apply to this debate. The decision of the Alberta supreme court was on the question whether or not Alberta had the power to make an order in council affecting the leasing of timber rights in Alberta, transferred to that province in 1930 by an act which this bill is designed to supplement. There is no analogy whatsoever between that situation and the one which confronts this parliament. What we are now trying to determine is whether or not this parliament of Canada has the authority to confer upon Alberta complete control over her resources. The second case to which the hon. member for Calgary West referred had to do, perhaps with the question as to whether or not this parliament had the power to pass on to Alberta the necessary powers. It certainly has nothing to do with the power of this parliament to pass this measure. I say that the matter for us to decide is whether or not we shall pass this measure. If, after we shall have passed the bill, a court

sees fit to rule that the legislation is invalid, then it will be the responsibility of the court. But as to the matter of passing the measure, and of endeavouring, in so far as in us lies the authority, to confer upon Alberta sovereign rights over her natural resources, I maintain that this dominion government unquestionably has that power to pass such an act, and should do so.
